chunks.text: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects derivatives and integrals, showing that differentiation and integration are inverse processes.
FTC Part 1: if F(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt with f continuous, then F'(x) = f(x).
FTC Part 1 means the derivative of an accumulation function equals the integrand evaluated at the upper limit.
The rate at which accumulated area grows equals the height of the function at the leading edge, like a tub filling at the current flow rate.
If the upper limit is a function g(x), FTC Part 1 with the chain rule gives d/dx ∫ from a to g(x) of f(t) dt = f(g(x))·g'(x).
Forgetting the chain-rule factor when the upper limit is g(x) is the most common FTC Part 1 error.
When the variable is in the lower limit, flip the integral first, which introduces a negative sign.
Example: if G(x) = ∫ from 0 to x² of sin t dt, then G'(x) = sin(x²)·2x = 2x·sin(x²).
Example: ∫ from 1 to x of (1/t) dt defines ln x, since its derivative is 1/x and it equals 0 at x = 1.
FTC Part 2: if F is any antiderivative of a continuous f, then ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).
FTC Part 2 lets you evaluate a definite integral by finding an antiderivative and subtracting its values at the endpoints, avoiding Riemann sums.
The notation F(x) evaluated from a to b means F(b) − F(a): top limit minus bottom limit.
No +C is needed in FTC Part 2 because the constant cancels: (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C) = F(b) − F(a).
Example: ∫ from 1 to 3 of x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3.
Example: ∫ from 0 to π of sin x dx = [−cos x] from 0 to π = 1 + 1 = 2, the area of one sine arch.
Indefinite integrals produce a family of functions and need +C; definite integrals produce a single number and do not.
If f(t) is velocity, ∫ from a to b of f(t) dt = F(b) − F(a) is the displacement, the final position minus the initial position.
The Net Change Theorem: ∫ from a to b of f'(x) dx = f(b) − f(a), so integrating a rate gives the net change in the quantity.
A final amount equals the initial amount plus the integral of the rate: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ from a to b of f'(x) dx.
FTC Part 1 says integration followed by differentiation returns the original function, a round trip.
FTC Part 2 says differentiation followed by integration recovers the net change in the original function.
Both parts express one idea about a tank: the flow rate is the derivative of total water, and the integral of the flow rate is the total water added.
